analysis.one_liner: Makes it easier to sue and prosecute police officers for misconduct and creates a national police misconduct registry.
analysis.headline: The George Floyd Justice in Policing Act of 2024 never received a committee vote or floor action before the 118th Congress ended, so it died without a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would change how police officers are held accountable in court. It would end "qualified immunity," the legal shield that usually protects officers from being personally sued when they violate someone's constitutional rights. It would also lower the bar for federal criminal prosecution of officers who knowingly or recklessly harm someone, ban racial profiling, ban no-knock warrants in drug cases, restrict chokeholds, and limit the transfer of military equipment to local police. It would create a public national registry of police misconduct records — complaints, discipline, firings, and lawsuits — and require police agencies to report detailed data on every use of force, with federal grant money withheld from states that don't comply. The bill never got a hearing or a vote in any committee and died when the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: People who live in communities where police misconduct and racial profiling are most common — disproportionately Black and Latino neighborhoods — gain a path to sue officers personally, a public searchable registry of officer misconduct records, mandatory reporting of every use of force, and restrictions on no-knock warrants, chokeholds, and military gear for police. Victims of sexual abuse by officers gain a new federal criminal penalty.

how_it_helps.text: It would end qualified immunity — the court-made doctrine that shields officers from being personally sued — for local and federal law enforcement officers accused of violating constitutional rights.
It lowers the federal criminal standard for convicting an officer of depriving someone's rights from 'willfully' to 'knowingly or recklessly' and makes death easier to attribute to the officer's act.

It creates a public National Police Misconduct Registry of complaints, discipline, terminations, and lawsuit settlements, searchable by the public, and ties federal grant money to states reporting use-of-force and misconduct data.

It bans racial profiling as a matter of federal law, lets individuals sue to stop it, and requires federal, state, and local agencies to collect and publish stop and use-of-force data broken down by race and ethnicity.

It bans no-knock warrants in drug cases, discourages chokeholds, restricts transfer of military equipment to local police, sets a federal use-of-force standard (the PEACE Act), and requires body cameras for federal officers.
It makes it a federal crime for officers to engage in sexual acts with people they have detained or arrested, closing what the bill calls the 'consent loophole.'

analysis.who_pays: Police departments and their unions bear the cost: easier civil suits against individual officers, a federal criminal standard that is easier to meet, public disclosure of misconduct records, mandatory use-of-force data collection, accreditation requirements, and possible loss of federal Byrne and COPS grant money for noncompliance.

drawbacks.text: Ending qualified immunity as a defense in federal civil-rights suits would expose individual officers to personal financial liability for good-faith mistakes in violent, fast-moving encounters — the chief objection raised by police unions and many law enforcement groups in the 2020 debate over the same provisions.

The bill changes the federal criminal civil-rights standard from 'willfully' to 'knowingly or recklessly,' making it easier to prosecute officers who cause death, which critics argue criminalizes judgment calls made under pressure.
The bill conditions existing federal policing grant money (Byrne and COPS grants) on compliance with accreditation, reporting, and anti-profiling requirements, penalizing states that decline.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill tackles a real gap: officers who injure or kill civilians often face no personal legal consequence because of qualified immunity and prosecutorial reluctance to charge fellow officers [S2]. The strongest good-faith objection is cost and overreach — police unions and many law enforcement groups argue that removing qualified immunity exposes officers to personal lawsuits for split-second decisions, and that a subjective use-of-force standard could make routine policing legally riskier. The bill's data and grant conditions also add reporting burdens to every police department in the country. An honest weighing: the accountability benefits are substantial and targeted at genuine documented harms, but the qualified-immunity change as drafted applies to good-faith conduct of any kind, which goes further than some reformers propose. The most immediate drawback is that none of it was enacted: the bill died in committee, so the status quo — including the legal doctrines the bill sought to change — remains.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to House committees, and never got a hearing or vote before Congress ended.

narrative.text: H.R. 8525 was introduced in the House on May 23, 2024, with 155 cosponsors, all Democrats.
The bill was referred to the House Judiciary, Armed Services, and Energy and Commerce committees, and then on May 31, 2024, to a Judiciary subcommittee; no further action appears in the record.
Congress.gov lists no committee vote, no floor vote, and no Senate action; the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, and the bill died there.
The bill's 155 cosponsors were exclusively Democratic, meaning it lacked the Republican support needed to advance in a House controlled by a narrow GOP majority.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Police unions and law enforcement agencies that opposed the 2020 version of this bill are better off, since the liability limits, data mandates, and grant conditions it would have imposed never became law. Nothing changed for families of people killed or injured by police.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Police unions and departments that opposed reform

for.name: 155 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors of the bill.

for.name: House Judiciary Committee and its Subcommittee on Innovation, Data, and Commerce
for.what_they_did: Held the bill after referral; the record shows no markup, hearing, or committee vote.

for.name: Republican House leadership
for.what_they_did: Allowed the bill to die in committee without floor consideration, as the House majority controls the legislative calendar.

sides.party_line_note: All 155 cosponsors were Democrats; no Republican sponsored or cosponsored the bill, and the Republican-controlled House never brought it to a vote.

industries.industry: Police departments and law enforcement agencies
industries.note: The bill imposes accreditation standards, use-of-force and racial-profiling data reporting, a national misconduct registry, and grant conditions on every level of law enforcement, and it widens the legal channels for suing departments and officers. Departments that fail to comply can lose federal Byrne and COPS grant money.

Collective bargaining agreements that block federal pattern-or-practice enforcement or conflict with consent decrees would cost a jurisdiction its federal grant money, and officers would lose qualified-immunity protection in civil suits — provisions unions opposed in earlier versions of this bill.

industries.industry: Law enforcement accreditation organizations and civilian oversight groups
industries.note: The bill steers federal grant money toward accreditation bodies like CALEA and funds civilian review boards and community organizations that monitor policing, giving them a funded, permanent role in police oversight.
